topic: selling an outcome, not an app: verified exception reduction instead of an agent demo
audience_job: decide whether to sell a measurable reduction of manual exceptions instead of an AI demo
experiment_variable: opening line: app generation versus business outcome
label: SOURCE_ANALYSIS

parts:
AI can generate an app. It cannot guarantee a business outcome.

NBER's revised survey: 78% of firms use AI, but executives report only a 0.2% annual productivity-growth boost.

Sell verified exception reduction, not an agent demo.

https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836

image_brief: The source draft recommends no image: it treats a 78% adoption and a 0.2% productivity figure as a dual-axis graphic that would mislead, and a decorative AI visual as less truthful than the source link. A card for this post would have to carry the claim without mixing denominators.

source_angles.thesis: Cheap app creation does not establish firm productivity; a builder should sell an auditable reduction of costly manual exceptions rather than only an agent demo.
source_angles.evidence: NBER Working Paper 34836 (October 2026 revision): nearly 9,000 executives across seven countries, 78% of firms use AI, executives estimate AI raised annual labor-productivity growth by 0.2% over the previous three years.
source_angles.counterexample: A buyer might prefer fixed-price software or staff training, and surveys average across firms rather than proving the service is profitable.

source_angles.thesis: As app generation becomes easier, connecting legacy data, error handling, approvals and compliance may retain cost and value.
source_angles.counterexample: Good horizontal platform vendors may bundle these functions, depressing margins.

source_angles.thesis: Generic AI adoption metrics do not predict ROI; target a narrower job or process and calculate task-level economics.
source_angles.counterexample: Micro-metrics can be gamed and may miss broader innovation benefits.
